title: Midlife Movement Pays Off Decades Later
hook: Exercise and healthy blood sugar in your forties and fifties tracked with slower cognitive decline decades on — and the benefit wasn't the same size for everyone.
key_points: Physical activity in midlife was linked to slower cognitive decline decades later.
Healthy blood sugar levels in midlife tracked with the same protective pattern.
The benefit of activity appeared especially strong for Mexican American adults.
That variation suggests brain-protective factors may differ across populations.
The window that matters is midlife — long before symptoms would appear.
content_html: A study looking at midlife habits and later brain health found two things worth acting on now: people who were physically active in midlife, and people whose blood sugar stayed in a healthy range, showed slower cognitive decline decades later.
extra_html:
Neither factor is a surprise on its own — both show up repeatedly in dementia-risk research. What's useful here is the timing. The exposures were measured in midlife and the outcomes appeared decades afterward, which reinforces that the window for protecting your brain opens long before anyone would think to worry about memory.

The researchers also flagged something less commonly reported: the benefit of physical activity appeared especially pronounced for Mexican American adults. Most large cohort studies of brain aging have been built on predominantly white populations, and findings like this are a reminder that the protective factors may not carry the same weight for everyone. It's a nudge toward more representative research as much as a finding in its own right.

related.title: Keeping Your Brain Healthy
related.hook: No pill prevents dementia, but the habits that protect your heart turn out to protect your brain too.

related.title: Nearly Half of Dementia Risk Is Something You Can Change
related.hook: A long-term brain study tied smoking, high blood pressure, heart disease, and high blood lipids to the damage behind vascular dementia — risks that are all treatable.

related.title: The Link Between Diabetes and Dementia
related.hook: Diabetes and dementia keep turning up together — and it may be no coincidence. Trouble with insulin and blood sugar can starve, inflame, and damage the brain's blood vessels.
